name: Rucking

lead: Rucking means walking or hiking with a weighted backpack. It comes from military loaded marches and has become a fitness trend. People take it up as a lower-impact alternative to running to lose fat, build conditioning and work the back, legs and posture muscles for a stronger-looking frame.

The added load raises the energy cost of walking and the demand on legs, trunk and posture muscles, and proponents say it adds bone-loading stress and calorie burn well above unweighted walking. Claims rest mostly on general exercise-physiology reasoning, and no trials of civilian rucking for appearance outcomes were located.

paras: Users load a pack with a light weight and walk or hike for short sessions, then build up distance and load over time, usually a few times a week as a replacement for jogging.
Leg injuries and heat exhaustion are reported in military loaded marching. For civilians, the sources describe starting with a light load and short sessions.

social.title: Rucking is an easy way to fitness

web.title: Rucking is an easy way to fitness - Hacker News

angle.text: Walking with a loaded pack burns more calories than plain walking and loads the back, legs and posture muscles, supporting fat loss and a stronger-looking frame. Appearance-specific trials have not been done.

lead: Rucking is walking or hiking with a weighted backpack (a rucksack) as exercise. The term comes from military loaded marches; the civilian version is promoted as a way to turn ordinary walking into a more demanding workout without running [1][2][3]. People use it to burn more calories than unweighted walking, to build leg and back muscle, and to work on posture, all of which feed into a leaner, more athletic-looking physique.

Cleveland Clinic sports medicine physician Matthew Kampert describes rucking as urban hiking, and the clinic's page says it can burn up to three times the calories of unweighted walking, roughly comparable to jogging, with faster pace and heavier loads raising the burn [3]. In physique circles it is discussed as a low-impact alternative to jogging for fat loss, and lifters on T Nation mention rucking alongside running and calisthenics as conditioning [4][5].

Research that uses the term mostly concerns military load carriage and, separately, the rugby 'ruck.' One randomized trial in recreationally active young men tested ruck performance with a pack weighing 30% of body weight [6], and a foot-biomechanics study examined backpack load in soldiers with mild flatfoot [7]. No trial has examined civilian rucking for appearance outcomes.

paras: In civilian form, rucking is deliberate weighted walking for fitness. One description holds that it needs a natural walking or hiking gait, an external load carried in a backpack, and an intent to train, which separates it from treadmill walking with added weight or weighted-vest walking [2]. It is also distinguished from recreational hiking, from multi-day backpacking, and from military ruck marches with timed standards [2].
Workouts are described by pack weight, distance and duration [3].

A loaded march is a relatively fast march over distance while carrying a load. The US Army and Canadian Forces say 'ruck march', the British Army 'tab', the Royal Marines 'yomp', the Australian Army 'stomping' and the US Marine Corps 'hump' [1]. Wikipedia cites the Roman writer Vegetius as describing loaded marches in recruit training, and notes modern standards vary by country; the US Army Expert Infantryman Badge requires 19 km within three hours with a load of up to about 31.75 kg [1].

Grokipedia gives energy expenditure figures of roughly two to three times unweighted walking and says rucking builds muscular endurance and bone-loading stress; it also notes brisk walking allows longer sessions with lower injury risk [2]. Cleveland Clinic reports that studies of adults aged 65 to 74 found weighted step exercises improved leg strength, power and daily function, and that 10 weeks of weighted walking plus resistance training improved physical performance [3]. Sources vary in the calorie figures they give.

Wikipedia notes that leg injuries are common during loaded marching in military basic training and that heat exhaustion limits marches in some climates [1]. Kampert warns that starting with heavy loads or long distances can lead to injuries such as stress fractures, that loose weights in an ordinary backpack can strain the shoulders and lower back, and that people with painful bone or joint problems should check with a healthcare provider [3]. A 2022 study of soldiers with mild flatfoot examined how backpack load changes foot motion and plantar pressure [7].

A 2023 Hacker News thread on a CNN article about rucking drew two comments, one asking about joint safety [8]. On T Nation, members log trail rucks and loaded runs, and one member who had been thinking about rucking considered adding a backpack to dog walks [4][5].

No studies found of civilian rucking for body composition or appearance. A randomized trial in recreationally active men found that either a ketogenic or a carbohydrate bar eaten three hours earlier allowed about an hour of exhaustive incline rucking with a pack at 30% of body weight [6]. Research on weighted walking in older adults is summarized by Cleveland Clinic [3].

lore.intro: Rucking is described in fitness media and by lifters as a beginner-friendly way to add intensity to walking [3][4].

claims.claim: Rucking burns far more calories than walking and nearly as many as jogging.
Rucking improves bone density and muscular endurance.
Loaded marching carries injury risk when load or distance rises quickly.
